title: Approximability of Unit-Demand Capacitated Vehicle Routing
short_statement: In capacitated vehicle routing, the classic iterated tour partitioning gives ratio $\alpha+1$ ($\alpha$ = best TSP ratio). A 2021 breakthrough shaved off a tiny amount; whether the $+1$ can be reduced - ideally to match TSP - is open.
open_problem: Determine the optimal approximation ratio for unit-demand capacitated vehicle routing in general metrics, and in particular whether the classical $\alpha+1$ barrier can be substantially improved.
background: Capacitated vehicle routing is a fundamental routing model in operations research. In the unit-demand version, a depot and customers lie in a metric space, every customer has demand one, and each vehicle tour may visit at most $Q$ customers before returning to the depot. The classical iterated tour partitioning algorithm starts with a TSP tour and cuts it into capacity-feasible pieces, yielding ratio roughly $\alpha+1$, where $\alpha$ is the best metric-TSP approximation ratio. That guarantee stood for decades. Blauth, Traub, and Vygen gave the first improvement, shaving a fixed constant from the $\alpha+1$ bound for general, unit-demand, and splittable variants. The resulting open problem is how much of the extra $+1$ capacity loss is inherent, and whether CVRP approximability can be pushed much closer to TSP.
full_statement: In unit-demand capacitated vehicle routing, the input is a finite metric space with a distinguished depot $r$, a set of customers $C$, and an integer vehicle capacity $Q$. Each customer has demand one. A feasible solution is a collection of tours, each starting and ending at $r$, such that every customer is visited by some tour and each tour visits at most $Q$ customers. The objective is to minimize total tour length. Let $\alpha$ denote the best approximation ratio known or achievable for metric TSP. Classical iterated tour partitioning gives ratio $\alpha+1$ by building a TSP tour through all customers and cutting it into capacity-feasible routes. Determine the optimal approximation ratio for unit-demand CVRP in arbitrary metrics. In particular, decide whether one can substantially beat the tour-partitioning barrier, perhaps approaching the TSP ratio plus a smaller capacity-overhead term, or prove that a large additive loss over TSP is inherent.
known_results: Haimovich and Rinnooy Kan's iterated tour partitioning gives an $\alpha+1$ approximation for unit-demand CVRP, where $\alpha$ is the approximation ratio for metric TSP; Altinkemer and Gavish obtained related partitioning guarantees. This was the benchmark for about 35 years. Blauth, Traub, and Vygen prove the first improvement, obtaining $\alpha+1-\epsilon$ for an explicit positive constant, and their result applies to unit-demand CVRP, splittable CVRP, and general CVRP variants in arbitrary metrics. Hardness is much weaker and largely inherited from metric TSP, so the true threshold could be near $\alpha$, near $\alpha+1$, or somewhere between. Recent work improves other unsplittable CVRP variants, but the clean unit-demand approximability threshold remains open.

progress.summary: The classical $\alpha+1$ barrier has been beaten by a small constant, but no near-tight algorithmic or hardness threshold is known.

counterexample_rationale: Hard instances for route partitioning, LP relaxations, or proposed algorithms are finite metric instances and can be evaluated exactly for moderate size.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can find metric instances where partitioning-style algorithms lose close to their bounds and suggest better route decompositions.

literature.synthesis: The $\alpha+1$ guarantee separates routing cost into a TSP backbone plus depot-return/capacity overhead. The Blauth-Traub-Vygen improvement shows that this decomposition is not tight in the worst case, but the improvement is small. A major challenge is to integrate capacity decisions into the tour construction rather than partition after the fact. Lower bounds are also underdeveloped: known hardness does not explain an additive $+1$ loss. Progress may come from stronger route-covering relaxations, better randomized partitioning, or hard metric families where depot-distance and intercustomer-distance terms conflict.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Search for bad instances for iterated partitioning and for newer randomized partitioning schemes. Algorithmic routes include LP/route-cover relaxations, depot-distance decompositions, and coupling with improved TSP rounding.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: State whether the claim is for unit-demand, splittable, unsplittable, or arbitrary-demand CVRP; these variants have different guarantees and reductions. A unit-demand result must handle arbitrary metric spaces and arbitrary capacities $Q$, and each route may serve at most $Q$ customers. For lower-bound instances, certify the optimum CVRP value, not just the performance of tour partitioning. For algorithmic claims, separate the TSP-approximation component from the capacity-overhead analysis.
